name: Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2)
priceNote: from $379 (Headliner/Wayfarer); Skyler/Wayfarer variants ~$409; prescription + Transitions add cost
audioNote: 5-mic array, louder/deeper bass vs Gen 1; some leakage in quiet rooms
camera: 12 MP ultrawide, 3K video @ 30fps, clips up to 3 min
subscriptionNote: Meta AI free for now; some AI/live-translation features US/region-limited
battery: built-in ~8 h mixed use; charging case adds ~48 h
platform: Meta AI app (iOS / Android); Meta/Facebook or Instagram account required
dataStorage: photos/video sync to Meta AI (Meta View) app and Meta cloud; voice queries and 'Look and ask' images processed on Meta servers; AI-training opt-out available since 2025 in some regions
privacyNote: Meta account mandatory; capture LED is small and easily missed; voice + images leave the device to Meta unless AI features are disabled.
standout: The default pick: best build, biggest ecosystem, most polished capture; also the most locked to one company.
notes: Gen 2 doubles battery, adds 3K/slow-mo video and 'conversation focus'. Still no display - that is the separate Meta Ray-Ban Display.

name: Ray-Ban Meta Skyler (Gen 2)
priceNote: from $409; cat-eye style with a smaller/narrower fit
audioNote: same 5-mic array and speaker system as the Gen 2 Headliner/Wayfarer
subscriptionNote: Meta AI free; feature availability varies by region
battery: built-in ~8 h mixed use; charging case adds ~48 h
platform: Meta AI app (iOS / Android); Meta account required
dataStorage: identical to Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 - capture syncs to Meta cloud, AI queries processed on Meta servers
privacyNote: Same Meta account + cloud-AI model as the rest of the line; differs only in frame shape/size.
standout: The Gen 2 for smaller faces / cat-eye styling; specs otherwise match the mainline Ray-Ban Meta.
notes: Essentially a frame-style SKU of the Gen 2 platform rather than a distinct product.

name: Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 1)
priceNote: launched $299; still discounted at retail while stock lasts, being replaced by Gen 2
audioNote: 5-mic array; quieter and thinner-sounding than Gen 2
camera: 12 MP ultrawide, 1080p video @ 30fps, ~60 s clips (later extended to 3 min via update)
subscriptionNote: Meta AI added by software update in 2024; free
battery: built-in ~4 h mixed use; charging case adds ~32 h
platform: Meta AI app; Meta account required
dataStorage: capture and AI queries go to Meta cloud, same model as Gen 2
privacyNote: Same Meta account + cloud dependency; included for context as the outgoing model.
standout: The product that made camera glasses mainstream; now superseded by Gen 2.
notes: Context entry. Gen 2 is the current SKU at the same frame styles.

name: Oakley Meta HSTN
priceNote: standard from $399; Limited Edition launched at $499
audioNote: louder open-ear speakers than Ray-Ban Meta; 5-mic array
subscriptionNote: Meta AI free; region-limited features
battery: built-in ~8 h mixed use; charging case adds ~48 h
platform: Meta AI app (iOS / Android); Meta account required
dataStorage: same Meta cloud pipeline as Ray-Ban Meta - capture syncs to Meta, AI queries processed on Meta servers
privacyNote: Oakley styling on the identical Meta platform; same account lock-in and cloud AI.
standout: Ray-Ban Meta internals in a sportier lifestyle frame with a bolder look.
notes: Runs the same Meta AI stack; the Vanguard is the more sport-focused sibling.

name: Oakley Meta Vanguard
priceNote: flat $499; single wraparound sport style, prescription NOT supported
audioNote: louder speakers tuned for wind/outdoor; 5-mic array with wind reduction
camera: 12 MP centre-mounted ultrawide, 3K video @ 30fps; Garmin/Strava overlays via app
subscriptionNote: Meta AI free; Garmin watch pairing optional
battery: built-in ~9 h mixed use; compact charging case adds ~36 h; IP67
platform: Meta AI app; Meta account required; optional Garmin Connect / Strava integration
dataStorage: capture and AI to Meta cloud; workout metrics pulled from paired Garmin device into the Meta AI app
privacyNote: Same Meta account + cloud model; centre camera makes recording direction less obvious to others.
prescriptionSupport: no (only non-Rx / reader inserts, wrap curvature too high)
standout: The cycling/running Meta glasses - IP67, wind-tuned audio, fitness overlays, biggest battery of the line.
notes: No prescription support is the main catch for many buyers.

name: Amazon Echo Frames (3rd gen)
priceNote: $269.99 list; frequently discounted to ~$200; prescription styles and sunglasses available
audioNote: directional open-ear drivers with auto-volume; leakage low but bass limited; no camera
subscriptionNote: Alexa works free; no sub needed, but cloud Alexa account required
battery: built-in ~6 h audio / ~14 h light use; charging via included cable, no case
platform: Alexa app (iOS / Android); Amazon account required; also passes through phone assistant
dataStorage: voice requests recorded and processed in Amazon's Alexa cloud; history stored in the Amazon account unless deleted / auto-delete enabled; no camera data
privacyNote: No camera lowers the risk; still an always-listening (wake-word) mic tied to Amazon's cloud and account.
prescriptionSupport: yes (order Rx lenses through Amazon partner)
standout: Lightweight audio-only Alexa glasses - the pick if you explicitly do NOT want a camera.
notes: Third gen is the current model; Amazon has not announced a successor as of 2026.

name: Solos AirGo 3
priceNote: from $199; modular 'SmartHinge' frame fronts sold separately (~$50-90 each)
audioNote: swappable temples with speakers; decent for calls/podcasts, light on bass; IP67
subscriptionNote: SolosChat (GPT-4o) usage free within limits; heavier use may need a paid tier
battery: built-in ~10 h; USB-C charge, no case
platform: Solos AirGo app (iOS / Android); routes AI queries to OpenAI
dataStorage: voice queries transcribed and sent to OpenAI via Solos servers; no camera; conversation history in the Solos app
privacyNote: No camera; mic-only. AI queries leave the device to third-party (OpenAI) cloud.
standout: Modular audio glasses with swappable styles and ChatGPT voice, cheap entry point.
notes: AirGo Vision is the camera-equipped sibling.

name: Solos AirGo Vision (AirGo V)
priceNote: from $299; camera temple module; swappable frame fronts extra
audioNote: same open-ear driver system as AirGo 3
camera: 13 MP stills, 1080p video; used mainly for 'visual AI' / describe-what-I-see
subscriptionNote: AI (GPT-4o / Gemini selectable) free within usage limits
battery: built-in ~10 h audio, much less with camera use; USB-C
platform: Solos AirGo app; images sent to OpenAI or Google for analysis
dataStorage: captured images uploaded through Solos to OpenAI/Google for visual answers; not a general photo-capture device; history in the app
privacyNote: Camera present but framed as an AI sensor; capture still routes to big-tech cloud models.
standout: Adds visual AI to the modular Solos platform at well under Meta pricing.
notes: Camera quality is modest; this is not a lifestyle-photo device.

name: Lucyd Lyte (2025)
priceNote: $149; many frame styles; Rx lenses via Lucyd optical partner
audioNote: 4-speaker array, dual noise-cancelling mics, Bluetooth 5.2; basic sound quality
subscriptionNote: ChatGPT voice via the Lucyd app; free within fair-use limits
battery: built-in ~12 h; USB-C, no case
platform: Lucyd app (iOS / Android); AI routed to OpenAI
dataStorage: voice queries to OpenAI via Lucyd; no camera; minimal on-device retention
privacyNote: Mic-only, no camera. AI queries go to third-party cloud; otherwise a plain Bluetooth audio frame.
standout: The cheapest way into 'AI glasses' - really just solid budget audio glasses with a ChatGPT button.
notes: Publicly traded maker (LUCY); wide style range and prescription focus.

name: Chamelo Music Shield
priceNote: ~$260; electrochromic tint models (Aura, Shift) span ~$200-350
audioNote: adequate for outdoor workouts; ~6.5 h playback from a small 180 mAh battery
subscriptionNote: no AI assistant; app only controls lens tint and audio
battery: built-in ~6.5 h; USB-C
platform: Chamelo app (tint control) + phone Bluetooth audio
dataStorage: no camera, no cloud AI; app handles tint presets and firmware only
privacyNote: No camera, no always-on assistant, no cloud capture. Standout feature is electronically adjustable lens tint.
standout: Button/slider-adjustable electrochromic sunglass tint with open-ear audio; sport/outdoor niche.
notes: The tint tech, not the audio or AI, is the reason to buy.

name: MserSee Audio Glasses
priceNote: ~$30-50 on Amazon; generic open-ear Bluetooth sunglasses
audioNote: basic dual open-ear drivers; noticeable leakage; IPX rating low
subscriptionNote: none - no app, no AI
battery: built-in ~7-8 h; USB-C
platform: none - pairs as a standard Bluetooth headset
dataStorage: nothing captured; no app, no cloud
privacyNote: A dumb Bluetooth speaker in a sunglass frame. No sensors beyond a call mic.
standout: Floor-price open-ear audio sunglasses; included to show the low end of the category.
notes: Representative of many near-identical white-label Amazon brands (also e.g. FEIYOLD, Kissproperty).

name: Bose Frames (Tempo / Tenor / Soprano)
priceNote: were $199-249; DISCONTINUED - Bose exited the category and shut its AR platform in 2024. Clearance/used only.
audioNote: best-in-class open-ear sound for their era; strong bass, low leakage
subscriptionNote: Bose Music app; the 'Bose AR' motion/spatial platform was discontinued
battery: built-in ~5.5 h (Tempo) / ~3.5 h (Tenor/Soprano); pogo-pin charge cable
platform: Bose Music app (still functional for basic EQ); no ongoing development
dataStorage: no camera; minimal data; AR platform that used head-motion data is shut down
privacyNote: No camera and the cloud AR platform is gone; effectively just Bluetooth audio sunglasses now.
prescriptionSupport: yes (were available via partners; hard to get now)
standout: Still the audio benchmark for open-ear glasses, but abandoned - buy only if you find a deal and just want sound.
notes: Included as a discontinued reference point. No firmware/feature updates coming.

name: Razer Anzu
priceNote: launched $199.99; DISCONTINUED and pulled from Razer's store. Clearance/used only.
audioNote: 16 mm drivers, 60 ms low-latency mode for gaming; mediocre sound, heavy leakage - widely panned
subscriptionNote: Razer Audio app for EQ; no AI
battery: built-in ~5 h; USB-C
platform: Razer Audio app; standard Bluetooth otherwise
dataStorage: no camera, no cloud capture
privacyNote: No sensors of concern; discontinued Bluetooth audio glasses.
prescriptionSupport: yes (blue-light + polarized swappable; Rx via third party)
standout: Razer's one-and-done attempt at audio glasses; mainly of historical interest.
notes: Discontinued reference entry.

name: Meta Ray-Ban Display
priceNote: $799 including the Meta Neural Band EMG wristband; US-only at launch, phased rollout
audioNote: 2 open-ear speakers, 6-mic array; used for calls, Meta AI, live captions/translation
subscriptionNote: Meta AI free; some features US-only; no subscription for core use
battery: built-in ~6 h mixed use; charging case adds ~24 h; Neural Band ~18 h separate
platform: Meta AI app; Meta account required; controlled by the Meta Neural Band (surface EMG wristband), not touch or voice alone
dataStorage: capture + AI queries to Meta cloud like the rest of the Ray-Ban Meta line; EMG wristband gesture data processed on-device/in-app
privacyNote: Everything the camera-only Meta glasses do, plus a screen. Meta account mandatory; capture and AI go to Meta's cloud.
standout: The first mainstream consumer HUD glasses with a colour display, sold with a neural wristband controller.
notes: 600x600 px, 42 PPD, 90 Hz panel / 30 Hz content. 20 deg FOV is small - notifications/nav/viewfinder, not immersive AR. Separate product from the display-less Ray-Ban Meta. Meta is reported to be developing "Name Tag" — opt-in facial recognition that would identify people and surface info via Meta AI — but it is not shipping and would reverse Meta's long-standing no-face-recognition policy.
personalMemory: none (reported: "Name Tag" facial recognition in development)

name: Even Realities G1
priceNote: launched $599, cut to $499; +$150 for prescription lenses; two frame shapes (A round, B rectangular)
audioNote: no speakers and no microphone - fully silent device; all input is via the phone or the touch temple
subscriptionNote: core HUD (notifications, nav, teleprompter, translate) free; some cloud features use the phone's connection
battery: built-in ~1.5 days typical; charging case adds several full charges
platform: Even Realities app (iOS / Android); pairs to phone, uses phone for connectivity and translation/transcription
dataStorage: text for translation/transcription is processed via cloud services through the app; no camera, no audio capture on the glasses themselves
privacyNote: No camera, no mic, no speaker on the device - among the most privacy-respecting smart glasses. Cloud use is limited to text features you trigger.
prescriptionSupport: yes (+$150, custom-ground into the waveguide lens)
standout: Looks like normal glasses; discreet green HUD for notifications, navigation, teleprompter and live translation with zero camera/mic.
notes: 640x200 per eye. Superseded by the G2 but still sold at a lower price.

name: Even Realities G2
priceNote: $599 (G2 A and G2 B); prescription lenses extra; R1 ring controller sold separately
audioNote: still no speakers; G2 adds a microphone for on-device voice notes / AI queries and dictation
subscriptionNote: HUD features free; AI assistant ('Even AI') uses cloud LLM via the app, free within limits
battery: built-in ~all-day; case ~48 h total; IP65
platform: Even Realities app (iOS / Android); optional R1 ring for gesture control
dataStorage: voice for AI/dictation is sent to cloud LLM/transcription via the app; no camera; user can avoid AI features and keep it mic-silent in practice
privacyNote: Still no camera. New mic is opt-in for AI/notes; without it the glasses stay a silent HUD.
standout: The refined G1: brighter, lighter, IP65, 75% bigger display area, adds a mic for AI without adding a camera.
notes: 640x350 per eye. The privacy-first display-glasses benchmark.

name: Halliday Smart Glasses (G1)
priceNote: from ~$369-499 depending on batch/frame; ships with an optional control ring
audioNote: small open-ear speakers + mics for calls and the proactive AI assistant
subscriptionNote: 'proactive AI' assistant free at launch; runs on cloud LLM via the phone app
battery: built-in ~8-12 h; charging case
platform: Halliday app (iOS / Android); AI via cloud LLM; ring or touch control
dataStorage: voice queries and conversation context sent to cloud AI via the app; no camera; transcripts/history in the app account
privacyNote: No camera, but always-available mic feeding a cloud AI assistant, plus an account. Lower risk than camera glasses, higher than Even Realities.
standout: Tiny near-eye module mounted at the top of the lens rather than a full waveguide; 'proactive' AI that volunteers info.
notes: Display is a very small monocular projector viewed by glancing up; not a full-field HUD.

name: Halliday G2
priceNote: $599; camera-free by design, aimed at meeting-room / office use
audioNote: open-ear speakers + mic array for real-time captions, translation and AI meeting notes
subscriptionNote: AI meeting features free within limits; heavier transcription use may require a paid plan
battery: built-in ~12 h; charging case
platform: Halliday app; cloud LLM + transcription
dataStorage: meeting audio transcribed and summarised via cloud services through the app; explicitly no camera; transcripts stored in the account
privacyNote: Deliberately camera-free, but it records and uploads meeting audio to the cloud for transcription - a real consideration in meetings.
standout: Moves to a real dual microLED waveguide; positioned as discreet office eyewear with live captions and AI notes, no camera.
notes: Newer/less independently reviewed; specs partly from vendor.

name: Brilliant Labs Frame
priceNote: $349 (clear/smoke/grey); optional prescription inserts
audioNote: microphone only, no speakers; audio responses come from the paired phone
camera: low-res camera (~1-2 MP class) for AI vision, not photography
subscriptionNote: 'Noa' AI assistant has a free tier; a paid Noa Pro plan exists for higher usage / better models
battery: built-in ~ hours; 'Mister Power' clip-on charger adds charges
platform: Open-source: firmware, hardware and the Noa app are on GitHub (github.com/brilliantlabsAR); MicroPython/Lua scriptable over BLE; works with custom backends
dataStorage: by default AI queries + camera frames go to Brilliant Labs' Noa service (which brokers to OpenAI/Perplexity/etc.); because it is open you can point it at your own or a local model
privacyNote: Camera + mic and default cloud AI, but fully open source - you can self-host the backend or run offline, which no big-tech option allows.
standout: The hacker's smart glasses: cheap, open hardware/firmware/app, scriptable, can be pointed at a local LLM.
notes: Display and camera are both low-spec; this is a dev/experimentation platform, not a consumer capture device. Successor is the Halo.

name: Brilliant Labs Halo (Halo X)
priceNote: $299 pre-order (some listings $349); ships ~Q1 2026; successor to Frame
displayTech: 0.2" microOLED, retro/arcade-style UI, +2 to -6 diopter adjust
audioNote: bone-conduction speakers + dual mics for the Noa assistant (not open-ear)
camera: AI-inference only (no photo/video capture, no capture LED)
subscriptionNote: Noa AI free tier + optional paid plan, same model as Frame
battery: built-in, up to ~14 h; USB-C
platform: Open source (firmware + app on GitHub); designed to run agents and to be retargetable to other AI backends
dataStorage: default cloud AI via Brilliant's Noa service; open enough to self-host or run against local models
privacyNote: Always-on camera + mic feeding a persistent personal knowledge base. Mitigations: camera cannot save media, an on-device Alif B1 NPU does some inference, and the stack is open source / self-hostable. Recording others into your memory graph is still an ethical/legal question in workplaces.
standout: The only shipping product built around remembering people and conversations: the "Narrative" agentic-memory system recalls names, prior conversations and context on the HUD. Audio/vision based, not facial recognition.
notes: Narrative is patent-pending; Noa builds a private personalised knowledge base from what you see and hear over time ("decades-long memory"). Alif B1 (Cortex-M55 + NPU) does light on-device AI; heavier queries go to Noa cloud (self-hostable because open source). Independent testing thin as of late 2026.

name: Vuzix Z100
priceNote: ~$499; also sold as a developer / OEM reference platform
audioNote: no speakers, no camera; notification/nav text only
subscriptionNote: no subscription; uses the phone app / SDK
battery: built-in ~2 days light notification use; USB-C
platform: Vuzix Connect app + open developer SDK; brand-neutral, no account lock-in
dataStorage: displays data pushed from the phone; no capture hardware, nothing uploaded by the glasses
privacyNote: No camera, no mic, no speaker - a pure notification HUD. Very low privacy footprint.
standout: Ultra-light micro-LED waveguide HUD from a long-time waveguide maker; developer-friendly and lock-in-free.
notes: Uses Vuzix's own micro-LED + waveguide (incognito). Mono green, text-focused.

name: Rokid Glasses
priceNote: ~$399 (roughly 280-380 EUR by market); AI + display + camera in a normal-looking frame
audioNote: open-ear speakers + mic array; used for calls, teleprompter, live translation and AI
camera: 12 MP, video up to 4K per some listings (typically used for AI vision + short clips)
subscriptionNote: AI assistant (Rokid + partner LLMs) free; some features region-specific (strong in China market)
battery: built-in ~ full day light use; charging case
platform: Rokid app; Snapdragon AR1; cloud AI via app; Rokid account
dataStorage: photos + AI vision frames + voice sent to Rokid cloud (and partner LLM providers); account-based history
privacyNote: Camera + mic + cloud AI with a Chinese-vendor account; capture LED present. Comparable exposure to Meta but a smaller/less-scrutinised data operation.
standout: Cheapest 'does everything' pair - dual green HUD, 12 MP camera, AI and translation - in an ordinary frame.
notes: Green mono display good for nav/teleprompter/subtitles, not media. Spec sheet varies by region/listing.

name: INMO GO2
priceNote: ~$399-599 depending on bundle/region; marketed heavily for live translation
audioNote: open-ear speakers + mics; core use is bilingual live subtitles shown in the lenses
subscriptionNote: translation uses cloud engines via the app; free tier plus possible paid quota for heavy use
battery: built-in ~ hours of continuous translation; charging case
platform: INMO app; cloud speech + translation services; INMO account
dataStorage: spoken audio is streamed to cloud ASR/translation providers via the app; no camera; transcripts may be retained in the app
privacyNote: No camera, but continuously captures and uploads nearby speech for translation - relevant when others are talking.
standout: Purpose-built translation glasses - dual green subtitle display, no camera.
notes: GO2 has no camera (unlike INMO Air/GO3 variants). Naming across INMO's line is confusing.

name: INMO Air 3
priceNote: ~$699; standalone Android AR glasses (no phone required)
audioNote: open-ear speakers + mics; on-board Android UI navigated with a ring/touch
subscriptionNote: runs apps on-device; AI features use cloud via Wi-Fi
battery: built-in (standalone); external battery/charging accessory available; runtime is short under load
platform: On-board Android (INMO OS); app store; INMO account for AI/cloud
dataStorage: self-contained for local apps; AI + any cloud apps send data out over Wi-Fi to INMO / third parties
privacyNote: Standalone (can run offline for local apps), but has a camera and cloud AI when connected; Chinese-vendor account.
standout: A full standalone Android AR computer in glasses form - no tethered phone or puck.
notes: Heavier and lower-res than tethered birdbath glasses; battery life is the main weakness of standalone designs.

name: RayNeo X3 Pro
priceNote: ~$1,199-1,299 (roughly 1,200 EUR); standalone AR glasses with on-board compute
audioNote: open-ear speakers + mic array; on-device assistant and spatial UI
camera: dual cameras (SLAM + capture), ~12-16 MP class stills, 1080p+ video
subscriptionNote: on-board Snapdragon compute; AI features use cloud when connected; no mandatory sub
battery: built-in (standalone); ~ a few hours active AR; USB-C charge; optional external battery
platform: On-board Snapdragon AR platform + RayNeo OS/app; RayNeo account for AI/cloud
dataStorage: SLAM/tracking on-device; captured media and AI queries go to RayNeo cloud / partner LLMs when online
privacyNote: Camera + mic + cloud AI, Chinese-vendor account. On-device compute means basic AR works offline.
standout: One of the first true standalone colour microLED-waveguide AR glasses at a sub-$1,300 price with real see-through optics.
notes: Full-colour waveguide with high brightness; distinct from the display-only RayNeo Air series.

name: RayNeo X2
priceNote: ~$699 (developer/early-adopter release); superseded by X3 Pro
audioNote: open-ear speakers + mics; on-board assistant, translation and navigation
subscriptionNote: AI/translation via cloud; no mandatory sub
battery: built-in (standalone) ~ a few hours; USB-C
platform: On-board Snapdragon AR1 + RayNeo app; RayNeo account
dataStorage: capture + AI/translation to RayNeo cloud / partner services
privacyNote: Camera + mic + cloud AI with vendor account; dimmer/narrower than the X3 Pro.
standout: First-gen standalone colour microLED waveguide glasses; heavy and low-FOV but proved the concept.
notes: Context/older entry; X3 Pro is the current model.

name: Vuzix M400
priceNote: ~$1,499-1,899 depending on config/volume; enterprise sales channel
audioNote: speaker + 3-mic noise-cancelling array tuned for loud industrial sites
subscriptionNote: hardware unlocked; remote-support software (Vuzix, TeamViewer, VSight, etc.) is separately licensed by the customer
battery: hot-swappable removable battery ~2 h; optional external battery pack on the headband
platform: Android (AOSP) on-device; MDM-manageable; customer chooses the remote-assist/workflow software and where it sends data
dataStorage: no consumer cloud - data goes wherever the enterprise's chosen software sends it (often the customer's own tenant / on-prem); can run fully on the local network
privacyNote: Camera + mic, but no built-in big-tech cloud or account; the deploying company controls data flow and can keep it on-prem.
standout: The workhorse assisted-reality headset for field service, warehouses and remote expert calls.
notes: Monocular puck that clips onto safety glasses or a headband; not lifestyle eyewear.

name: Vuzix Blade 2
priceNote: ~$1,299.99; enterprise-oriented but sold individually
audioNote: stereo speakers + noise-cancelling mics
subscriptionNote: hardware unlocked; workflow/remote-assist software licensed separately
battery: built-in ~2-3 h; USB-C; external battery pack optional
platform: Android on-device; MDM support; customer-chosen software and data destination
dataStorage: as with the M400 - data routes through the enterprise's chosen application; can be kept on the local network
privacyNote: Camera + mic but no built-in consumer cloud; enterprise controls the pipeline.
standout: Glasses-shaped (not puck) enterprise AR with a bright see-through waveguide; entry price for a real waveguide headset.
notes: More wearable than the M400 but lower camera spec; both are enterprise tools.

name: RealWear Navigator 520
priceNote: ~$2,000-2,700 per unit depending on config/volume; enterprise channel only
audioNote: loud mono speaker + 4-mic array engineered for 100+ dB industrial noise; fully voice-driven ('assisted reality')
camera: 48 MP stills, 4K video, image stabilisation; detachable camera module
subscriptionNote: device unlocked; RealWear Cloud / remote-assist and 3rd-party apps are separately licensed
battery: hot-swappable removable battery ~ a full shift with spares
platform: Android (RealWear); voice-only UI; MDM; runs Teams/Zoom/TeamViewer/etc.; customer controls data destination
dataStorage: no consumer cloud; video/photos and call streams go to the enterprise's chosen platform, which can be self-hosted / regional
privacyNote: Camera + mic, but no big-tech account or default cloud; built for controlled industrial deployments.
prescriptionSupport: yes (mounts over safety glasses / hard hat)
standout: The rugged, fully hands-free 'assisted reality' headset for frontline workers in noisy/hazardous environments.
notes: Not eyewear - a helmet/headband-mounted display boom. Navigator 520 sharpens the image and widens FOV vs the 500.

name: Rokid X-Craft
priceNote: ~$2,000-2,800 enterprise pricing; IP66, ATEX/explosion-proof options
audioNote: speakers + noise-cancelling mic array; helmet-mountable
camera: 48 MP stills, 4K video; plus depth/thermal add-on options
subscriptionNote: device unlocked; remote-assist / inspection software licensed by the customer
battery: hot-swappable battery; external pack; full-shift with spares
platform: Android (Rokid) on-device; MDM; customer-selected software and data routing; supports on-prem
dataStorage: enterprise-controlled; can operate on a private network with no external cloud
privacyNote: Industrial tool; camera + mic but no consumer account/cloud by default.
standout: Ruggedised, explosion-proof AR headset for energy, chemical and heavy industry.
notes: Helmet-form, not glasses-form; included for enterprise context.

name: Magic Leap 2
priceNote: Base ~$3,299; Developer Pro and Enterprise tiers higher (with support/warranty)
audioNote: spatial-audio speakers + mic array; dynamic dimming lets it work in bright rooms
camera: 12.6 MP RGB + multiple tracking / depth cameras
subscriptionNote: Enterprise tier bundles a software/support subscription; base hardware has none
battery: external compute puck (tethered) ~3.5 h; puck holds the battery + chipset
platform: Android-based (Magic Leap OS); OpenXR; enterprise-managed; on-prem deployment supported
dataStorage: no consumer cloud; enterprise controls data; can run offline / on private infrastructure
privacyNote: Sensor-dense but enterprise/dev-only, no consumer account, data flow is customer-controlled.
standout: Widest FOV and best optics of any see-through AR headset in this list, with segmented dimming; included for context.
notes: Tethered to a hip-worn compute puck; a headset, not glasses, and enterprise/developer focused.

name: XREAL One
priceNote: $499; XREAL Eye camera add-on ~$99; XREAL Beam Pro compute puck sold separately
audioNote: open-ear speakers tuned with Bose; mics only on the optional Eye module
camera: none built-in (optional clip-on XREAL Eye adds a camera for capture / 6DoF)
subscriptionNote: no subscription; Nebula app is free
battery: none - draws power from the connected device over USB-C; needs a phone/PC/console, or an XREAL Beam Pro puck for standalone use
platform: Plugs into any USB-C DP device; XREAL X1 chip does 3DoF anchoring on-glasses without a host app; Nebula app for Android/Mac/Windows
dataStorage: acts as an external monitor - it shows whatever the host device outputs; the glasses themselves capture and upload nothing (no camera/mic by default)
privacyNote: With no built-in camera or mic it is effectively a wearable display. Privacy depends on the host device, not the glasses.
standout: Best all-round display glasses: on-board X1 chip pins a virtual screen in space with no host software, wide 50 deg FOV.
notes: Not standalone - always needs a source device or the Beam Pro. Camera is opt-in hardware.

name: XREAL One Pro
priceNote: $599 ('forever price'); Eye camera + Beam Pro puck extra
audioNote: Bose-tuned open-ear speakers; flatter/wider prism optics for a bigger image
subscriptionNote: none
battery: none - USB-C powered by the host; needs a source device or XREAL Beam Pro for standalone
platform: USB-C DP into any compatible device; X1 chip for 3DoF; Nebula app
dataStorage: external display only; no capture hardware by default
privacyNote: Same as XREAL One - a display, not a sensor. Camera is an optional accessory.
